    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09892v1</id>
    <title>On Agentic Manipulation Policies</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:59:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09892v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09892v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1</id>
    <title>CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:58:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09891v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09887v1</id>
    <title>On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:58:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09887v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09887v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$, for a bounded connected open set $Ω\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$ or in $C(\overlineΩ)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09882v1</id>
    <title>FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:56:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09882v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09882v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. A B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state space while enforcing temporal smoothness, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each agent's predictions on observed neighbor motion for interaction-aware forecasting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, outperforming deterministic baselines on joint position error, pose error, and final displacement error despite producing a full predictive distribution. We additionally establish the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose, a large-scale professional soccer dataset, where social conditioning demonstrably concentrates predictive uncertainty along interaction-constrained directions.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09878v1</id>
    <title>Graded convolutional networks: scale invariance without the scale and robustness to unknown blur</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:54:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09878v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09878v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Gaussian jet of an image is a graded vector space: a dilation by $λ$ multiplies derivatives of order $k$ by $λ^{-k}$. Local graded convolutions are exactly homogeneous differential operators, and a local feature is dilation-invariant if and only if it factors through the scale-normalized jet or, without the scale, through the retraction onto the weighted sphere of the grading. Under unknown Gaussian blur the retraction changes only by a change of scale, whereas the scale-normalized jet acquires a grading factor that no radial normalization removes. At the zero jet the retraction separates image families that radial normalizations and continuous classifiers cannot. Networks built on the retraction are universal for invariant features. On MNIST such a network keeps 88.4% accuracy under a two-pixel blur, against 66.2% for the same network on scale-normalized derivatives; in Lindeberg's Gaussian derivative network the retraction raises accuracy at that blur from 91.5% to 95.1%.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09876v1</id>
    <title>Novikov-Magnus Master Equation for Driven Quantum Systems under Classical Correlated Noise</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:53:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce a modular framework for deriving time-local quantum master equations for driven systems subject to temporally correlated classical noise. The construction combines the Donsker-Furutsu-Novikov relation with the Magnus expansion: Functional response closes the noise average, while nested commutators retain the noncommuting chronological action of noise-induced perturbations along the controlled quantum trajectory. For zero-mean Gaussian noise, we derive the resulting Novikov-Magnus quantum master equation through fourth order in the noise strength. The same response hierarchy suggests a natural extension beyond Gaussian noise, with connected higher-order noise correlations weighting higher functional derivatives of the stochastic map. For a driven qubit under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and band-limited $1/f$ noise, the second- and fourth-order maps remain CPTP throughout the perturbative regime and accurately reproduce stochastic simulations. Their diamond-norm errors are comparable to those of the cumulant-based pseudo-Lindblad master equation, with a modest fourth-order improvement for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09873v1</id>
    <title>Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:49:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09873v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09873v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated $1/f$ noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09872v1</id>
    <title>On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:49:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09872v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09872v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09866v1</id>
    <title>GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:47:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09866v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09866v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
  Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation.
  Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
  Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09864v1</id>
    <title>Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:44:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09864v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09864v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/</summary>

    <title>Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:44:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09863v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09863v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings.</summary>

    <title>A Quantum Mechanical Description of Active Matter</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:42:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09861v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09861v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Furthermore, living systems broadly employ periodic, non-repeating motion for both locomotion and various biological functions, with meaningful information stored in the periods of these functions. Consequently, analyzing these dynamics in the Fourier space lands us at the familiar tools of the operator based, quantum mechanics. This is accomplished by introducing a complex field to describe the evolving probability distribution of a single unit, as well as the population density of mutually non-interacting active particles under the constraint of scarce resources. The resulting single-unit wavefunction evolves analogously to the Dirac equation with minimal coupling, wherein gauge symmetry reflects the generality of the governing equations across arbitrary resource landscapes. Additionally, we present a Schrödinger-like equation where the effective potential term represents the environmentally mandated, non-motile base metabolic rate. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.</summary>

    <title>Raman anyon-Hubbard model in a 1D Bose lattice gas</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:38:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09855v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09855v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The anyon-Hubbard model is the paradigmatic lattice model of one-dimensional (1D) anyons, in which chiral interactions make bosons equivalent to particles with fractional statistics. Its continuum limit, the chiral BF theory, emerges as the low-energy description of a Raman-coupled Bose gas with imbalanced interactions. Here, we show that loading such a gas into a 1D optical lattice realizes the lattice counterpart of this theory, which we name the Raman anyon-Hubbard model. The Raman-dressed bosons acquire density-dependent Peierls phases when tunneling through occupied sites. For a small statistical phase, the model reduces to the anyon-Hubbard model, while beyond this limit it defines a distinct lattice anyon model with unbounded rather than periodic statistical interactions. Numerically, we show that the dressed gas displays the defining properties of 1D anyons, namely a density-dependent asymmetry of the ground-state momentum distribution, interaction-induced asymmetric transport and chiral bound states. Remarkably, these features are readily accessible with Raman-coupled $^{39}$K atoms, opening up the experimental exploration of 1D anyons beyond the few-particle regime.</summary>

    <title>Classical control of quantum-state relaxation in confined molecular hydrogen</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:34:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09850v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09850v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum-state conversion between the ortho and para nuclear-spin states of H$_2$ is forbidden in the isolated molecule but these states can become connected through interactions with a surrounding environment. How that same environment governs the dynamics of the newly connected states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this problem using H$_2$ confined in crystalline molecular solids, where the host environment selectively enables conversion between a pair of otherwise disconnected ortho-H$_2$ and para-H$_2$ states. Rotationally resolved infrared spectroscopy directly determines the state-specific conversion dynamics in crystalline CO$_2$ and N$_2$O at 10 K, revealing that increasing H$_2$ concentration suppresses nuclear-spin conversion by nearly an order of magnitude, reaching complete suppression by 20% H$_2$ loading. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations identify two complementary origins of this concentration dependence: changes in the thermally populated phonon modes available to mediate relaxation, and strain-driven H$_2$ clustering that progressively removes molecules from the host crystal field responsible for enabling conversion. The resulting picture connects a classical collective response of the host to microscopic quantum-state dynamics: H$_2$ loading generates strain that reorganizes the local molecular environment, thereby modifying both the phonon bath and the molecular coupling to that bath. These results establish a multiscale mechanism by which condensed-phase environments can govern the connectivity and dynamics of an effective two-level system.</summary>

    <title>Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:31:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09847v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09847v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI.     <summary>The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive's ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation.     <title>Gibbsian Entropy for General Wigner Distributions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:25:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09839v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09839v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose a definition of non-equilibrium Gibbsian entropy applicable to general quantum systems, computable from Wigner functions, for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states. We show that while the Wigner function is a quasi-probability distribution, fundamental results linking observables in repeated observations to the function, such as the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem and, crucially, the relation between the entropy and the cumulant generating function continue to apply. This ideas are the core of the large deviation theory, which allow to formulate a positive-definite definition of entropy based on our ignorance of the underlying state structure after repeated measurements of cumulants. This new definition is a parallel to the Gibbs entropy formulation, but it can also be used in out-of-equilibrium regimes. Some important properties of this entropy are discussed. In addition we derive some information theory quantities such as relative entropy, conditional entropy, mutual information and Rényi entropy. We then compare the results with Wehrl entropy for the 1D harmonic oscillator, for pure and mixed states. We conclude the the work discussing potential applications of this new formalism, ranging from quantum correlations beyond entanglement to thermalization in closed quantum systems.</summary>

    <title>Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:23:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09836v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09836v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.</summary>

    <title>Deterministic Quantum Search for NP Problems Through Verifier-Based Oracle Construction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:16:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09830v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09830v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Problems in the class NP are important in computational science, where a given candidate solution can be verified in polynomial time, while finding a solution may require evaluating the entire search space in the worst case. Classical exhaustive approaches generally solve such problems by evaluating the verifier function over all possible inputs, resulting in a worst-case query complexity of O(N), where N = d^n represents the size of the search space, d is the number of possible values for each variable, and n is the number of variables. Quantum search algorithms can solve unstructured search problems more efficiently by reducing the query complexity to O(sqrt (N)), providing a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive search. However, conventional quantum search formulations typically assume access to an oracle that identifies valid solutions, while standard implementations generally yield probabilistic success. In this work, we propose a generalised quantum oracle construction method for NP problems, together with a deterministic quantum search framework that identifies satisfying assignments using their corresponding classical verifier functions. The proposed framework retains the quadratic query speedup of quantum search over classical exhaustive search. We further establish that constructed oracle can be implemented using a number of gates polynomial in the size (L) of the binary encoding of verification function, consistent with the polynomial-time evaluation of the corresponding classical verifier, while the total qubit requirement remains O(poly(L)). The construction is demonstrated on multiple N-SAT instances, with circuit-level simulations confirming deterministic identification of satisfying assignments. These results establish the applicability of deterministic quantum search to NP problems while retaining the quadratic query advantage over classical exhaustive search.</summary>

    <summary>Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.</summary>

    <summary>The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.</summary>

    <title>Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:08:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09822v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09822v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.</summary>

    <title>Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:06:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09818v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09818v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.</summary>

    <title>The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:02:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09815v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09815v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.</summary>

    <title>Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T18:01:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09814v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09814v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When does a quantum particle arrive at a detector? The temporal distributions of itinerant quantum particles have been debated since the birth of quantum mechanics. Here we study the arrival-time problem in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. The arrival dynamics exhibits two regimes, the quantum Zeno and the low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. In support of the theory, on superconducting quantum hardware, we measure arrival-time distributions for single and multiple interacting particles in one- and two-dimensional circuits. The measured distributions resolve both regimes and agree closely with quantum-trajectory theory. The crossover persists in interacting many-particle systems: the optimal monitoring point is preserved while many-body interference reshapes the distributions. Zeno suppression likewise persists in two-dimensional geometry. Together, these results show that the two regimes are a generic feature of monitored propagation rather than a single-particle effect. To our knowledge, our work constitutes the first experimental measurement of arrival-time distributions in a monitored quantum transport setting, addressing one of the longest-standing problems in quantum mechanics.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09809v1</id>
    <title>Beyond the $n/2$ Threshold: Quantum Query Complexity for Computing Hamming Weight and Symmetric Functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:58:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09809v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09809v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The oracle-interrogation algorithm [van Dam, FOCS '98] computes every $n$-bit Boolean function with bounded error using $n/2+O(\sqrt n)$ quantum queries. In contrast, parity can be computed exactly using $\lceil n/2\rceil$ queries, but whether an additive overhead beyond $n/2$ is necessary for a single Boolean output has remained open. In this work, we construct an explicit family of symmetric Boolean functions requiring $n/2+Ω(n^{1/3})$ quantum queries at a fixed positive constant error. We also give an algorithm that recovers the exact Hamming weight using $n/2+O(n^{1/3})$ quantum queries with bounded error, and therefore computes every symmetric Boolean function within the same query bound. Together, these results determine the optimal additive order for Hamming weight recovery and for the worst case over symmetric Boolean functions at sufficiently small constant error.</summary>

    <title>Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:55:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09805v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09805v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09802v1</id>
    <title>When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:54:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09802v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09802v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.</summary>

    <title>Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:54:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09803v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09803v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.</summary>

    <title>Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:53:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09798v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09798v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.</summary>

    <title>Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:46:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09792v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09792v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.</summary>

    <title>Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:46:28Z</updated>

    <summary>Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.</summary>

    <title>Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:44:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09785v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09785v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.</summary>

    <title>Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:42:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09779v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09779v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09778v1</id>
    <title>Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:40:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09778v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09778v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $ρ>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $ρ$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09773v1</id>
    <title>A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:36:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured that every bounded polynomial of low degree on the discrete cube has an influential variable. They showed that the conjecture implies that the acceptance probability of every quantum algorithm making $T$ queries can be approximated on most inputs by a classical algorithm making $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ queries. We prove their conjecture: every function $f\colon\{-1,1\}^n\to[-1,1]$ of degree at most $d\ge1$ has a variable of influence at least $c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^{5/2}/d^{6}$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. In the original formulation, for polynomials of degree at most $d$ with values in $[0,1]$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ and variance at least $\varepsilon$, this gives a variable of influence at least $(\varepsilon/d)^{7}$. The proof is elementary, with steps inspired by works of others. Thus, as Aaronson and Ambainis anticipated, superpolynomial quantum speedups in the query model require structure, such as a promise on the inputs.</summary>

    <title>ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:32:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09770v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09770v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09768v1</id>
    <title>Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T17:31:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09768v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.09768v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.</summary>

* At screening, receipt of a PI-based regimen with no regimen change for a minimum of 24 weeks prior to screening.
* Confirmation of VF of current second-line PI-based ART. NOTE A: Failure of the current second-line regimen was defined as two consecutive measurements of plasma HIV-1 RNA ≥1000 copies/mL obtained at least 1 day apart while on the current PI-based regimen. "Current PI-based regimen" and "current regimen" were understood to be the regimen described (ie, the regimen that the candidate was taking when the first VF sample was drawn plus only those modifications allowed).
* CD4+ T-cell count result from a specimen drawn within 103 days prior to study entry
* Laboratory values obtained within 30 days prior to study entry:

  * Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 500/mm\^3
  * Hemoglobin ≥7.5 g/dL
  * Platelet count ≥40,000/mm\^3
  * Creatinine ≤2 X upper limit of normal (ULN)
  * Aspartate aminotransferase (AST), serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT), and alkaline phosphatase ≤5 x ULN
  * Total bilirubin ≤2.5 x ULN
  * Creatinine clearance (CrCl) \>30 mL/min, either measured or estimated by Cockcroft-Gault equation
  * Hepatitis B panel that includes HbsAB, HBcAB, and HBsAG or only HBsAG, with plasma stored for later anti-HBs and anti-HBc.

NOTE A: Candidates who were eligible for cohort B and who were positive for active hepatitis B infection were assigned to sub-cohort B3 at registration/randomization.

NOTE B: Candidates with CrCl \<60 mL/min who were also positive for active hepatitis B infection were not eligible.

* Females of reproductive potential (women who have not been post-menopausal for at least 24 consecutive months, ie, who have had menses within the preceding 24 months, or women who have not undergone surgical sterilization, hysterectomy or bilateral salpingectomy or bilateral oophorectomy or tubal ligation) must have had a negative serum or urine pregnancy test prior to the submission of the screening genotype testing sample and again within 48 hours prior to randomization or registration.
* Female participants of reproductive potential must have agreed not to participate in the conception process (ie, active attempt to become pregnant, in vitro fertilization), and if participating in sexual activity that could lead to pregnancy, the female participant must have used at least one reliable form of contraceptive. Acceptable forms of contraceptives included:

* Condoms (male or female) with or without a spermicidal agent
* Diaphragm or cervical cap with spermicide
* Intrauterine device (IUD)
* Hormonal contraception

1. Other primary cancers apart from non-melanoma skin cancers, carcinoma - in situ of the cervix, or a prior cancer treated with curative intent more than 2 years ago without any evidence or recurrent disease

6. Clinically-significant uncontrolled cardiac arrhythmia other than asymptomatic atrial fibrillation not requiring therapy.

Subjects will be asked to complete a Geriatric Assessment (GA). GAs are designed to gather information on memory, nutritional status, mental health, and level of social support. GAs are also designed to help the health care team understand how well subjects can carry out their day to day activities and to briefly describe what other medical conditions subjects may have. Researchers want to understand if chemotherapy changes the levels of p16 in blood.","detailedDescription":"This multicenter Phase II clinical study will investigate the complete response (CR) rate after therapy with bendamustine combined with rituximab in older (≥65 years old) patients with previously untreated stage II-IV DLBCL deemed poor candidates for cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine (Oncovin®), prednisone, rituximab (CHOP-R); n=37. The hypothesis being tested is that this regimen will be safe and effective as frontline therapy in older DLBCL patients deemed poor candidates for CHOP-R. After 3 cycles of therapy, patients with less than a partial response (PR) will come off study, and be managed at the discretion of their treating physician. Patients who achieve a PR after 3 cycles will continue for a total of 8 cycles of therapy, while patients who achieve a CR will continue for a total of 6 cycles of therapy. Secondary objectives include overall response rates (ORR), disease-free, progression-free and overall survival, and an evaluation of the toxicity and tolerability of the regimen.

This trial also includes an exploratory analysis designed to evaluate a potential correlation between expression of the senescence marker p16INK4a and the toxicity associated with this regimen.

Of these, approximately 3 to 5% will develop into an acute, painful form of fibrosis. Mild fibrosis can present as a thicker or more dense breast where the acute form can cause pain in the breast, significant hardening, and inflammation.

Treatments for fibrosis are lacking, with the primary treatment being hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The combination of Trental \& Vitamin E has been used with success in Europe and at the University of Iowa.

1. Female age ≥ 18 years
2. High-grade serous epithelial ovarian, primary peritoneal, or fallopian tube cancer
3. Measurable disease per RECIST Version 1.1
4. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score 0-1
5. The subject's tumor tissue must be positive for cyclin E1 protein expression per the Sponsor's clinically validated cyclin E1 IHC investigational, in vitro diagnostic assay
6. Prior Therapy:

   1. Subject must have platinum-resistant disease
   2. One to 3 prior lines or regimens are allowed (1 to 4 prior lines are permitted, if prior mirvetuximab)
   3. Prior bevacizumab treatment is required, if eligible per standard of care
   4. Prior PARP inhibitor treatment is required if BRCA 1/2 mutation or HRD, if eligible per standard of care
   5. Prior mirvetuximab treatment is required, if eligible per standard of care
7. Adequate hematologic and organ function during the screening period

Exclusion Criteria:

1. History of another malignancy in the previous 2 years, unless cured by surgery alone and continuously disease-free. Exceptions include appropriately treated carcinoma in situ of the cervix, nonmelanoma skin carcinoma, Stage 1 uterine cancer, or other malignancies with an expected curative outcome.
2. Subjects with primary platinum-refractory disease.
3. Prior therapy with azenosertib or any other WEE1 inhibitor, ATR inhibitor, CHK1/2 inhibitor, or (PKMYT1) inhibitor for PROC.
4. A serious illness or medical condition(s) including, but not limited to, the following:

   1. Clinically or radiographically unstable brain metastases or leptomeningeal disease that requires immediate treatment. Subjects with asymptomatic brain metastases are eligible.
   2. Acute kidney injury requiring intervention, or presence of indwelling urinary catheter or percutaneous nephrostomy.
   3. Significant gastrointestinal abnormalities, including an inability to take oral medication, requirement for IV alimentation, active peptic ulcer, chronic diarrhea or vomiting considered to be clinically significant in the judgment of the Investigator, or prior surgical procedures affecting absorption.
   4. Any evidence of small bowel obstruction as determined by air/fluid levels on computed tomography (CT) scan, recent hospitalization for small bowel obstruction within 3 months before randomization, or recurrent paracentesis or thoracentesis within 6 weeks before randomization.
   5. Active, uncontrolled infection. Subjects with an infection receiving treatment (antibiotic, antifungal, or antiviral) must have completed such treatment and the infection must be considered controlled/resolved (and afebrile) by the Investigator for at least 7 days before randomization
   6. Myocardial impairment of any cause resulting in heart failure by New York Heart Association criteria (Class II, III or IV).
   7. Medical or psychiatric condition or laboratory abnormality that may increase the risk associated with study participation or may interfere with the interpretation of study results
5. Any of the following treatment interventions within the specified time frame before randomization:

   1. Hospitalization within 14 days
   2. Major surgery within 28 days
   3. Any chemotherapy or targeted tumor therapy within 21 days or 5 half-lives (whichever is shorter)
   4. Radiation therapy within 21 days
   5. Autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplant within 3 months
   6. Current use of any other investigational drug therapy \< 28 days or 5 half-lives (whichever is shorter)
6. Inability to discontinue treatment with prescription or nonprescription drugs that are prohibited per protocol.
7. Inability to discontinue consumption of food and herbal supplements that are prohibited per protocol
8. Prior wide-field radiotherapy affecting ≥ 20% of the bone marrow.
9. Unresolved toxicity of Grade \> 1 attributed to any prior therapies (excluding Grade ≤ 2 neuropathy, alopecia, or skin pigmentation).
10. Subjects who are immunocompromised or HIV-positive on highly active anti-retroviral therapy
11. Subjects with known active hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection

I. Determine the dose-limiting toxicity and maximum tolerated dose of AFP464 in patients with advanced solid tumors.

II. Assess the safety and tolerability of this drug in these patients.

I. Observe clinical response in patients treated with this drug. II. Characterize the pharmacokinetics of this drug in these patients. III. After salvage HDT half of the patients receive maintenance therapy with carfilzomib/dexamethasone while the other half are observed without maintenance therapy.","detailedDescription":"The survival in younger myeloma patients improved in the nineties with the introduction of high-dose melphalan with autologous stem cell support (HDT) and despite the emergence of novel therapies HDT remains a keystone in myeloma treatment. However, all patients will eventually experience relapse after HDT performed at diagnosis. Eligible patients with late relapse are considered for salvage HDT. The duration of response after salvage HDT is in most studies reported to be approximately half the length of the response after initial HDT. The choice of induction treatment before HDT might affect the outcome after the induction therapy as well as the outcome after the HDT. In other settings the novel proteasome inhibitor Carfilzomib has showed superiority to the first-in-class proteasome inhibitor bortezomib. In addition, carfilzomib has a favourable profile of side effects. Thus, the aim of this phase 2 study is to evaluate induction therapy with carfilzomib-cyclophosphamide-dexamethasone before salvage HDT. The primary end-point in this part of the study is comparison of time to progression after the initial HDT and time to progression after salvage HDT when four series of carfilzomib-cyclophosphamide-dexamethasone are used as induction therapy. In the study Carfilzomib is also included in the conditioning regimen with administration of Iv carfilzomib 27 mg/sqm on day -2 and -1. The standard conditioning regime consists of Iv melphalan 200 mg/sqm on day -2 and reinfusion of at least 2.0 x 10m CD34+ stem cells/kg body weight on day 0.

The purpose of maintenance therapy in multiple myeloma is to prolong the time to progression of disease. There are limited data on the impact of maintenance therapy after salvage HDT. Another important aim of the study is therefore to evaluate the effect of carfilzomib/dexamethasone given every other week compared to observation without maintenance therapy. This part of the study starts two months after HDT. The randomization is stratified according to relapse 1 - 2 years or \> 2 years after HDT, ISS stage and standard versus high-risk cytogenetics. The primary end-point of this part of the study is comparison of time to progression in carfilzomib-dexamethasone maintenance arm and in the observational arm. Patients will continue on maintenance therapy/observation until progression, end of study or fulfil standard criteria for discontinuation of treatment according to the protocol.

The study will include 200 patients with relapse of multiple myeloma more than one year after initial HDT. It is a prerequisite that the patients have at least 2.0 x 10m CD34+ stem cells/kg body weight saved in the freezer. The study is conducted by the Nordic Myeloma Study Group (NMSG) at clinics in Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Lithuania. The first patient was included in January 2015 and enrolment is expected to continue until December 2017. Patients with newly diagnosed, symptomatic multiple myeloma based on the following criteria:

* Presence of an M-component in serum and/or urine plus clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow and/or a documented clonal plasmacytoma

PLUS one or more of the following:

* Calcium elevation (11.5 mg/dl) \[42.65 mmol/l\]
* Renal insufficiency (1.5 x the ULN of serum creatinine)
* Anemia (hemoglobin \<=10 g/dl or 2 g/dl \<= normal)
* Bone disease (lytic lesions or osteopenia)

Measurable disease is defined at least one of the following three measurements:

* Serum M-protein \>=1 g/dl ( or 10 g/l)
* Urine M-protein \>=200 mg/24 h
* Serum FLC assay: Involved FLC level \>=10 mg/dl (\>=100 mg/l) provided serum FLC ratio is abnormal
* Measurable plasmacytoma
* NOTE: If a patient meets the criteria for symptomatic multiple myeloma but does not meet serum M-protein, urine M-protein or serum FLC levels stated above, percent plasma cells in bone marrow will be used to follow response.

* Absolute neutrophil count \>= 1.0 x 109/L
* Platelet count \>= 50 x 10(9)/L
* Hemoglobin \>= 9 gm/dl
* Serum creatinine \<= 2.5mg/dL.
* Total bilirubin \<=1.5 x upper limit of normal
* AST (SGOT) and ALT (SGPT) \<= 3 x ULN

Exclusion Criteria:

* The development of erythema nodosum if characterized by a desquamating rash while taking thalidomide or similar drugs.
